Chapter 2: The Secret to Sleeping Through the Night
If you’ve ever faced the wild adventure of new parenthood, you know that sleep—or the lack of it—can feel like the ultimate test. In so many places, those sleepless nights are almost worn like a badge of honor. But what if there’s another way? Imagine a city like Paris, where babies often sleep through the night much sooner, and their parents don’t look quite so exhausted.
So, what’s their secret? It’s actually a pretty simple idea: babies can learn how to sleep, and parents can help them get there without endless rocking, late-night drives, or marathon feeding sessions. In France, they have a phrase for it—“doing the nights.” But don’t worry, it’s not about strict routines or letting babies cry for ages. It’s all about observation, patience, and a gentle confidence in what your child can do.
Picture this: in one family’s apartment, those first few weeks with a newborn were just as chaotic as you’d expect—nighttime feedings, groggy mornings, and that constant worry of “Am I doing this right?” But then, they started noticing how their French neighbors handled things. When their baby made a noise at night, these parents didn’t jump up right away. Instead, they paused—just for a moment—before stepping in. It seemed like such a tiny detail, but it turned out to make a world of difference.
Here’s something most people don’t realize: babies, just like us, move through cycles of light and deep sleep. Sometimes they fuss or whimper as they shift between cycles, but that doesn’t mean they’re fully awake. By waiting those few moments before responding, parents actually give their babies a chance to settle themselves. And as the nights go by, little by little, babies start piecing those sleep cycles together—stretching out their rest, and giving everyone in the house a little more peace.
It’s a small shift, but it changes everything. Parents start to trust not just their instincts, but their child’s natural resilience. And babies? They build the kind of self-soothing skills that will help them far beyond their crib years.
Of course, it’s not always smooth sailing. Some nights are tougher than others, and every child is unique. But at its heart, this approach is really about faith. Faith that your child can adapt, and faith in yourself to gently guide them—without hovering or overwhelming. It’s not about being cold or distant. It’s about creating a calm, predictable space where everyone can finally get some rest.
As the weeks go by, the shift is almost magical. The baby sleeps longer, parents start to feel more like themselves again, and the whole family finds a steady new beat. So, what’s the big takeaway? Sometimes, the best thing you can do is just wait, watch, and truly believe in your little one.
